speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: CONTINUANCE OF WEST INDIES TOKEN IMPORT PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a short announcement. I am glad to be able to announce that confirmation has been received from London that the West Indies token import plan is being continued for 1954. I also have word that a number of commodities of importance to Canadian trade are being added to those on open general licence in the West Indian colonies.
The list of commodities on open general licence will include: newsprint; kraft paper; dried, smoked, pickled and salted fish; onions; potatoes; cheese; powdered and canned milk; split peas; meats; canned fish. Animal feeds are also on the list except in British Guiana.
Several of these items were previously traded under token import plan vouchers in the colonies. They will now be unrestricted and vouchers will not be needed for them.
The West Indies token import plan is playing a valuable part in keeping Canadian brand names before the public in the colonies, and in holding a place in those markets for Canadian goods until the trade need no longer be restricted. The transfer of commodities from the plan to open general licence is an encouraging sign for the future.
Full details of these changes are being given to the trades concerned by my departmental officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO RESUPPLY OF WEATHER STATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement on the Arctic weather stations.
On March 4, 1947, announcement was made in the house that the Canadian and United States governments had decided to establish weather stations in the Canadian Arctic which were to be operated jointly by the Canadian meteorological service and the United States weather bureau. It was then announced that
the Canadian government would supply the required establishments and that the United States would furnish necessary water and air transportation.
That year a United States task force, sailing from Boston on July 15 and consisting of two icebreakers and a supply ship, made their way to Resolute bay on Cornwallis island and to Eureka sound on Ellesmere island. Weather stations were established at these two points. Since then three additional joint Arctic weather stations were established and have been in operation on a 24-hour day ever since. All these joint weather stations are located in the area now designated as Queen Elizabeth islands. For the first few years, the resupply of these Arctic stations was carried out from Resolute by the United States army air force but this airlift has gradually been taken over by the R.C.A.F.
With respect to transportation by sea to these Arctic outposts, Canada has been able to supplement the work of the United States task force during the last two summers. In 1952 the Department of Transport's Arctic supply ship, the C.G.S. C. D. Howe, delivered considerable supplies to Resolute; and last summer the department's new icebreaker, the C.G.S. d'Iberville, contributed greatly to the resupply of this main weather station.
It is my pleasure to be able to inform the house that this year, Canada will be able to assume full responsibility for the resupply of all but one of the joint Arctic weather stations. My department will, this summer, send up a task force consisting of two icebreakers, the department's Arctic supply ship, the C. D. Howe, a commercial dry cargo vessel and a commercial tanker.
The departmental vessels will be carrying out this special work in addition to their regular duties in Arctic and sub-Arctic waters. The icebreakers used will include the d'Iberville, N. B. McLean and Edward Cornwallis.
The C.G.S. C. D. Howe will carry out, as in previous years, the supplying of government outposts along the coasts of Baffin island, lower Ellesmere island as well as Resolute where she will rendezvous with the task force.
C.G.S. d'Iberville will be the commodore ship of the task force and will accompany the commercial dry cargo vessel and tanker

Fisheries
to Resolute. Last year this new icebreaker opened a new R.C.M.P. post at Twin Glaciers, half-way up the eastern shore of Ellesmere island. This year, ice conditions permitting, d'Iberville is scheduled to travel up the west coast of Ellesmere to Eureka sound and will also carry out resupply work to other Arctic posts, including Craig harbour.
The joint Arctic weather station at Alert on the northernmost tip of Ellesmere island will be resupplied by the United States task force which will be servicing American establishments in Greenland.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO RESUPPLY OF WEATHER STATIONS
speechtext: None other than these five.

subtopic: PURCHASE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA CANNED SALMON BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: PURCHASE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA CANNED SALMON BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement on the sale of Canadian canned salmon to the United Kingdom. Before the war a large part of the annual British Columbia pack was sold in the United Kingdom. During the war years almost the entire pack was sent to Britain. In the post-war years, however, the British found it increasingly difficult to find the dollars necessary for such purchases and so sales declined. In 1952 the British bought no Canadian salmon, and it looked as though there would be no British purchases in 1953.
When the Right Hon. R. A. Butler, Chancellor of the Exchequer, was in Ottawa last spring, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and I raised the matter with him. He eventually agreed to allocate $4J million for salmon purchases, which bought 205,000 cases. At the time he expressed the hope that the fishing industry would try to buy more British goods to enable Britain to earn the dollars to finance such purchases.
I repeated his words here in the House of Commons last spring, and I am glad to say that the fisheries association of British Columbia took immediate action on this suggestion. A committee was formed which canvassed every branch of the industry to see how British purchases could be increased. By August of last year this committee had prepared an order for $4) million of new British purchases of tin-plate, mechanical equipment for plants and boats, and fishing gear.

The committee felt that there might be more equipment available in Britain than they knew about, so early in September Mr. Kenneth Fraser, manager of the Imperial Cannery, was sent to England to visit the British manufacturers. At the end of September a trade delegation consisting of Mr. H. R. MacMillan, chairman of the board of B. C. Packers, Mr. John Buchanan, president of B. C. Packers, Mr. Roger Hager, president of the Canadian Fishing Company and myself went to London.
We found that Mr. Fraser had done a splendid job and had found a great deal of other first-class British equipment, competitive in price. Mr. MacMillan was so impressed that he wired back to Vancouver to have the purchasing agent of his logging enterprises come to Britain for a similar survey.
The delegation had wisely decided not to try to link their British purchases with any conditions for the sale of salmon, so there was no suggestion of barter or any quid pro quo arrangement. We did feel, however, that the British government should know of the way the industry was trying to help the British earn dollars. We first met the Right Hon. Lloyd George, minister of food, and found him most sympathetic. He told us that he had great demand from the British people for much more British Columbia salmon and would be happy to provide it if the dollars could be found. We next met the Right Hon. Peter Thorneycroft, president of the board of trade, who was most impressed with the action taken to increase the sale of British goods in Canada. He was pleased too that the delegation had found so wide a range of first-class equipment available at competitive prices. He felt it was the first time that a whole industry had made a deliberate effort to help the British to earn more dollars.
Finally, our high commissioner in London, Mr. Norman Robertson, and I met the chancellor. He was frankly delighted that his suggestion of the spring should have brought such positive results. He told us that, while it was not possible for him to allocate dollars for salmon purchase in the fall months because of other commitments, he would try to make dollars available in the spring.
I went on to attend the Colombo plan meetings in New Delhi, but the rest of the delegation spent another three weeks in Britain arranging for purchase of this equipment. The British press gave very favourable comment on the purpose of the mission. Perhaps I can quote one paragraph of a

speech made on December 2 by the Right Hon. Derick Heathcoat-Amory, minister of state, to show the impression made on the British cabinet. He said:
We welcomed very much a mission that came over here recently from the fishing industry of British Columbia. Here is a case where a whole Canadian industry recognized in a very practical way the value of increasing trade between our two countries. They came to see what the United Kingdom could offer in the field in which they were interested. When they went away, they seemed to be impressed with all they had seen-the wide range of goods that were of interest, from ships' chandlery to diesel engines, and they found us to be up to date and our prices competitive. They returned full of enthusiasm and important orders look like materializing which may run into several millions of dollars. Here I suggest is one more pail in the coffin of the myth that the United Kingdom only produces luxury goods at high prices. We would welcome immensely other missions of the same kind.
Two weeks ago the British government informed us that a bulk purchase of salmon would be made this month. While the amount was not made public, it is considerably larger than last year's purchase. A representative of the British ministry of food is now in Vancouver negotiating the purchase. In view of this happy outcome I can assure you that the fishing industry of British Columbia will continue to press its "Buy British" campaign.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I rise now simply to deal with two statements which I could have dealt with on a question of privilege but which, it seems to me, might properly be dealt with at this time. Our position in regard to this measure was fully, clearly and definitely stated in the debate on second reading, where we have dealt with this subject by vote. But I do wish at this time to deal with two statements that have been made.
I read in one periodical publication a statement that prior to the presentation of this measure in parliament I had privately indicated my support of the measure. I wish to say with the utmost emphasis that the statement made in the periodical containing that statement is wholly untrue. I wish to make it definite and to say with the utmost emphasis that I have never at any time, in private conversation or by any private exchange of opinions, taken any position different from that which I took when the measure came before the house.
Then I find also it has been said that I was consulted in regard to this, and that because of certain considerations I withdrew from a position I indicated I might take. Under the rules of parliament it is difficult to deal with a statement of that kind in adequately effective terms. Nevertheless I simply wish to say again with the utmost emphasis that this statement that has been made, and has been repeated, is utterly untrue.
I thought it had been disposed of by the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he made it clear that the government had taken full responsibility, and that there had been no discussion of any kind in regard to this measure. I wish to place it on record very definitely that until I was informed by the Prime Minister, as a matter of courtesy, just before the motion
Senate and House of Commons was placed on the order paper, that it was going to be done, I had no idea what this bill contained. And I am perfectly certain that the leader of the C.C.F. party and the leader of the Social Credit party are in precisely the same position.

I regret very much that the government has not seen fit to accept either of the two suggestions I made that this bill should be referred to a royal commission or to a select committee appointed for the particular purpose of dealing with this measure, which would have no power, no authority in either case, except to inquire into the facts and to make its recommendations to the government for subsequent submission to parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext: When the committee rose previously we were considering an amendment proposed by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Shall the amendment carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I submit to you that the amendment moved by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is clearly out of order. I base my submission on two main grounds. The first one is that it contravenes the rules concerning amendments. The second ground is that, as this bill is a money bill, the amendment, which I submit will possibly result in the imposition of a charge on the Canadian people, should have been contemplated by the terms of the resolution which was considered in committee of the whole before the bill was introduced, and that the present amendment clearly exceeds the terms of the resolution which received the approval of the committee of the whole.
In connection with the first ground, Mr. Chairman, I submit that the amendment offends in three ways the rules regarding amendments. First, it offends in that it is not really an amendment; second, it is not relevant; and, third, it offends in that it raises new matter which can only be raised by a distinct motion after notice. We have not had any notice.
I would direct your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that what we are asked to do here is as follows, and I am reading from the amendment as reported at page 1902 of Hansard:
That clause 2 of Bill No. 168 be renumbered as clause 3, and that the following clause be inserted as clause 2 . . .
Then follows the detail of that proposed clause 2. I shall not read that at the moment although I shall have occasion to do so later. I submit to you that that is not, in fact, an amendment to clause 2 at all. I think it is important for us to realize the position we are in or were in prior to the moving of this amendment. The question before the committee was "Shall clause 2 of the bill carry"? Clause 2 reads as follows:
This act shall come into force on the 1st day of April, 1954.
That is clause 2. The question before the committee was that clause. The amendment does not seek to amend clause 2. It seeks to delete it altogether and to substitute some other proposition. In that connection I would refer you to Beauchesne, third edition, page 129, rule 48:
When a question is under debate no question is received unless to amend it; to postpone it to a day certain; for the previous question; for reading the orders of the day; for proceeding to another order; to adjourn the debate; or for the adjournment of the house.
Then there are laid down clear rules as to what constitutes an amendment and it is stated that a mere negative does not constitute an amendment. What we are asked 83276-121
Post Office Act
to do here is not to amend clause 2 of the bill in order to substitute some other date for the coming into force of this act; what we are asked to do is to delete clause 2 altogether and to substitute something else for it.
Turning to the other grounds in connection with this matter of whether or not it offends the rules with regard to amendments, Mr. Chairman, I refer you to citation 344 of Beau-chesne's third edition, at page 136, which reads as follows:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed. Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the house the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
The law on the relevancy of amendments is that if they are on the same subject-matter with the original motion, they are admissible, but not when foreign thereto. The exceptions to this rule are amendments on the question of going into supply or ways and means.
This not being a motion to go into supply or ways and means, that exception does not apply. I therefore submit that this amendment clearly contravenes that rule on the relevancy of amendments which says that if they are on the same subject matter with the original motion they are admissible, but not when foreign thereto. What we are asked to do here is to substitute for clause 2, which concerns the date of the coming into force of the act, a new clause which deals with the question of postal rates applicable to magazines and newspapers. There could not be anything much more foreign to the subject matter of the original proposed clause 2. It therefore seems to me that the amendment is clearly out of order on the ground of relevancy.
May I also refer you, Mr. Chairman, to citation 354 of Beauchesne's third edition, which reads as follows:
An amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved.
Again the motion before the committee is: "Shall clause 2 carry?" The Postmaster General now asks us not to carry clause 2 dealing with the subject of the coming into force of the act but to change it altogether and to carry an amendment which deals with the question of postage rates on magazines and periodicals.
Then the third ground on which I say the amendment offends the rule regarding amendments is that it raises new matter. In the first place, I have submitted that it is not an amendment at all. In the second place, I have submitted that it is not relevant. In

Post Office Act
the third place I now come to the proposition that it raises new matter which can only be moved by a distinct motion alter notice. I refer you, Mr. Chairman, to citation 355 at page 139 of Beauchesne's third edition which cites the precedent as follows:
An amendment was ruled out because it raised a new question which could only be considered on a distinct motion after notice.
Beauchesne there cites as his authority the Commons Journals, volume LXVI, pages 109-11, where the proposition was laid down in the house in February, 1929. I am not going to read the lengthy record as it appears in the Journals at pages 109 to 111, but I respectfully suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if you will refer to that authority you will see that the proposition there set forth-and, I might say, always since accepted by the house-is authority for the point that I now put forward in opposition to this amendment.
I realize that from time to time amendments have been made in this manner in committee on a bill. For instance, I recall the amendment made just recently to the Senate and House of Commons Act where a new section was included; but I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that that was done by unanimous consent. Here unanimous consent was not asked for and I want to make it quite plain that unanimous consent is certainly not being given.
Then I should like to deal for a moment or two with the logic behind the situation. Here, for nearly a week we have been considering amendments to the Post Office Act which are confined to the question of letter mail. The reason for the rule that new matter can only be raised by a distinct motion after notice is to avoid the house's being taken by surprise and being asked to make up its mind on a question which has never been before it and about which it has had no opportunity for reflection.
That is exactly the ground on which the original authority was decided, the case I have referred to at pages 109 to 111 of the Journals of 1929. Here we were asked to consider the question of letter rates, an increase in the postage on letters. It is true that we dug out of the Postmaster General yesterday that there was also going to be an increase on postcards. But, sir, we had no indication at any time previously that the house was going to be asked to amend the Post Office Act with respect to the facilities extended to those who use the post office for posting periodicals and newspapers. There is indeed some question in the government's mind as to whether this provision will extend to newspapers.

I am dealing with the logic of the situation. We are asked to deal with a new matter which was introduced at five minutes to ten last night. The government itself does not even know what the effect of the amendment will be, as is obvious from the interchange which took place as recorded in Hansard for yesterday. I am not going to deal with that at length. I expect that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will have something to say about it. But it does establish clearly that there is disagreement between the ministers as to the effect of this amendment.
Furthermore, I can only suggest, if this matter was so late in coming to the attention of the government that they could not deal with it until five minutes to ten last night when they presented us with an amendment of which they only had two copies, with the result that the Leader of the Opposition and the Postmaster General were the only ones who had one, that nothing could establish more clearly that it not only is a contravention of the rules regarding amendments to present this to us at that time, but that it would most definitely and improperly take the house by surprise to be asked to deal with it. Apparently it was a last-minute decision on the part of the government to introduce it. They did not mind springing it on the house as a surprise, but I want to make it perfectly clear that we are fed up with the way in which this bill has been handled and the way in which we have been confronted with a constant series of surprises.
Although in some circumstances we might have been disposed to give unanimous consent to introducing this amendment at this stage, it has now been made clear that the government is exceeding the limits of all propriety, and we are going to insist that for a change the government abide by the rules which are in force for the conduct of the business of the house.
I come to the question of the second ground upon which I claim the amendment is out of order. What we have before us is a money bill, and an amendment to enlarge its terms is out of order unless it was contemplated in the terms of the resolution which preceded the bill. I am not going to go into the arguments, which are quite extensive, as to whether or not it is a money bill. I simply point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that the government has itself accepted the proposition that it is a money bill because they introduced it by way of a resolution. I accept that proposition. I point out further that a money bill is not only one which deals with ways and means but, for the purposes

of this rule, is one which imposes a charge upon the people. Because this measure raises the postage rates and thus imposes a charge upon the people, I assume it was on those grounds that the government decided it was a money bill and dealt with it as a money bill. I quite agree that that was a sound decision.
This proposed amendment was not hinted at in any way, shape or form in the resolution which preceded the bill. I should like to read that resolution. It is as follows:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to increase the rates of postage on letters posted in Canada from the first day of April. 1954,
(a)	on each letter for delivery within the postal area in which it is posted, from three cents to four cents for the first ounce or fraction of an ounce . . .
(b)	on each letter posted within one postal area for delivery in another postal area from four cents to five cents for the first ounce . . .
The resolution is confined exclusively to the rates of postage on letters. By the terms of the resolution the government has asked us to consider the expediency of introducing a bill to increase the charges for letters. There is no reference anywhere to the question of charges to or facilities available for those who use the post office for the postage of magazines and newspapers, which is the subject of the proposed amendment now before us.
The government may have sought to cover this point in the last clause of the proposed amendment. After stating that the Postmaster General may make regulations dealing with this matter, it provides that he may do so on the following terms:
. . . that the application of this section to the newspaper or periodical when so posted will not adversely affect the postal revenues.
It might be contended that since this will not upset the balance of ways and means it is not an enlargement of the terms of the resolution; but I point out that it is quite possible that the effect of this amendment would be to increase the charges made against those who use the facilities of the post office for posting magazines or newspapers. In that respect not only does it exceed the terms of the resolution which the house passed but it contravenes the rules on dealing with money bills. Here I should like to quote the authority of Beauchesne's second edition, citation No. 791, at page 225, which reads as follows:
The committee-
The reference is to the committee of the whole, which is this committee.
-cannot agree to any clauses involving payments out of the public funds, or imposing any tax or charge upon the people unless such clauses have been previously considered by resolution in committee of the whole.
83276-121J
Post Office Act
In other words, this proposed amendment should have been included as one of the subject matters in the resolution which preceded the bill and which was adopted by the committee of the whole house. I should also like to refer to Bourinot, fourth edition, which I might point out is an authority referred to throughout by Beauchesne. At page 503, after having dealt at some length with the general provisions regarding bills involving public aid or charges, he says:
The rule just cited also applies to the imposition of any state tax or charge upon the people or any class thereof.
As I have said, it is quite clear that the proposed amendment may well involve a charge upon those who use the mails for the purpose of posting magazines and newspapers. They are a class of people who would be subject to a charge, and therefore on the basis of the authority of Bourinot, page 503, the proposed amendment is clearly out of order.
There are a number of other citations which might be read in support of my submission, but I think for the time being I will let the technical case rest there. I would again like Your Honour to consider the logic and common sense of the matter. As I have said already, we have been exposed to a number of surprises in the course of our dealing with this bill, and last night this one, at five minutes to ten, was the last in a long series of surprises of the sort which the rules of the house were clearly designed to prevent. I suggest to you, sir, that in fairness to the committee, which is part of the House of Commons, the committee should not be asked to allow the government to continue to spring surprises on it in this improper manner, but that the government should now be required to abide by the rules of the house and should withdraw this amendment. Indeed, I suggest that while they are doing it it would be as well, and highly proper, if they would withdraw the whole bill, which in general has been dealt with by them in this same improper manner.

I congratulate the hon.
member for Kamloops, Mr. Chairman, on the excellent case he has made against the propriety of the amendment which was moved last night. My remarks will be much briefer than they might otherwise have been, owing to the fact that the member for Kamloops has quoted most of the citations that bear on this point. I have been checking off the ones I had, one by one, as he read them. However, there is still one important citation which he either overlooked, or perhaps out of his generous nature he left for me.

Post Office Act
I want to say that I recognize the possibility of someone from the government side answering some of the arguments the member for Kamloops has advanced. I say this, even though I am supporting the position taken by the hon. member, not to weaken any of his arguments but to make it clear to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration or anyone who speaks from that side that an answer to one of the points or even two does not demolish the third one. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration holds up three fingers, but he cannot demolish the third one.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext: You are expecting demolition.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
With regard to the first point made by the member for Kamloops, I would say he is correct in stating that the amendment proposed by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is not a proper amendment to clause 2 of the bill. He made his case well, and I think it stands.
However, it is true that the government could get around that by withdrawing the amendment, as an amendment to clause 2 of the bill, and introducing it as a new clause. I believe that could be done under citation 670 of Beauchesne's third edition. I suggest that, as I say, not to weaken the case of the member for Kamloops but to let the other side know they are not going to get anywhere by trying to make anything out of that argument. Technically, the member for Kamloops is correct, but it could be done in this other way, provided the other arguments the member for Kamloops has put up were not in the way.
The second argument which the member for Kamloops has made is again one that the government will try to attack, and of course, they will be satisfied that they are attacking it successfully, but in my view they will not. I refer to his argument that this is a money bill, and that it is not proper to introduce an amendment to a money bill which goes beyond the scope of the resolution preceding the bill itself. The government will argue, as the member for Kamloops has already pointed out, that in the very words of the amendment the government proposed to put in the bill there is the suggestion that the power given to the Postmaster General shall not be exercised if it would result in an adverse effect upon the postal revenue.
I point out, however, Mr. Chairman, that it is possible, under this proposed amendment, for certain periodicals or magazines to find that the amendment's provisions are to them an advantage. As a result of that advantage they might well increase their circulation, and as a result of that draw a greater subsidy

from the federal treasury. Every magazine or newspaper that is posted today is posted in part at public expense. There is an element of subsidy there. If the circulation of any newspaper or magazine is increased, a result of this subsidy is that the loss to the treasury will be increased to that extent. My contention is that even though the Postmaster General may say that this is not to result in any loss of postal revenue per unit, it could result in a loss in this other way. I submit the amendment could have the effect of upsetting the balance of ways and means of the treasury as a whole, and therefore the point the member for Kamloops made in that connection is valid. This amendment should not have been made since it goes beyond the scope of the money aspect of the resolution that preceded the bill.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I come to the third point raised by the member for Kamloops. I submit that on this point the government has not a leg to stand on. It has been made crystal clear in the house time and time again, especially when members of the opposition violated this point, that a bill amending one section or one part of an act does not open the whole act. What the government did in this case was to introduce a bill amending section 10 of the Post Office Act. Nothing could be clearer, because it was stated in the resolution that it was to be a bill dealing only with rates of postage on letters. When we got the bill based on the resolution, to all intents and purposes it was a bill of one clause. Clause 2 had to do with the date it comes into effect. There was just the one operative clause which amends section 10 of the Post Office Act, and nothing else.
I insist, Mr. Chairman, that by virtue of the ruling that has been made from the chair of this committee as well as from the chair of the house time and time again, the amending of one section of an act does not open the whole act. If such action does not permit members on this side of the house to discuss other sections of an act, certainly it is equally clear it does not permit the government to open up other sections of an act by an amendment of this kind. This amendment now before us does just that. It opens up section 11 of the Post Office Act, to which there was no reference in the original resolution, no reference in the bill and no reference in the speeches or announcements on this matter made by the government. I submit the amendment goes far beyond what is allowed by the rules of the house, and far beyond the rulings that have been made in this house time and time again. Whatever satisfaction the Minister of Citizenship and

Immigration may get out of trying to worm around the first two points made by the member for Kamloops, he is up against it when he comes to the third one. He cannot answer it at all.
The one citation which the member for Kamloops left for me is citation 671 in Beau-chesne's third edition. It is also citation 792 in Beauchesne's second edition, and follows citation 791 which the hon. member read a few minutes ago. This citation reads:
A new clause will not be entertained if it is beyond the scope of a bill . . .
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this amendment clearly goes beyond the scope of the bill which was laid before us, and the government has no right to introduce it in this way. The government has the right to give notice in the usual way, to announce the Governor General's approval and deal with it in a proper parliamentary way. I do not deny that for a moment. But I do deny the government's right to play fast and loose with the rules just because of their majority; I deny their right to try to do things in this way.
I shall have something more to say about the substance of the amendment if it is allowed to stand. I shall have something more to say on the kind of explanation that was made last night by the Postmaster General in the light of information I have received since, if the amendment stands. However, such an argument would be on the substance rather than on procedure. I could continue, but it seems to me that on the one main issue the case is so clear you have no alternative, Mr. Chairman, but to say to the government that the amendment goes beyond the scope of the bill. It opens up a section of the Post Office Act which was not opened up by the original resolution, or by the bill, and therefore is not in order as an amendment moved in committee of the whole in this way.

night by unanimous consent. It was not done by unanimous consent. I have read the record since he spoke and I see in it no reference to unanimous consent.

speechtext:
I will come to that.
The first argument therefore is, I suggest, entirely out of court for the reasons I have given.
Then, the second argument is that, this being a money bill, therefore we should not amend it and thereby, as I take it, add another burden to the public charge of Canada. That of course is a matter of opinion-as to whether the result of this bill would be a public charge. Indeed, if I remember correctly, during the course of his explanation last night, in referring to the amendment the Postmaster General said that we would save money in doing this, rather than spend it. I am paraphrasing this, because he did not add the latter part of what I have said. However, he did say that we would have a saving. I do not think he added the additional negative-that we would not spend any more. However, I think that is what he meant.

Post Office Act
That being the case, I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that there is not an additional charge, and that it is not necessary that this should have been covered in the original resolution. Practically every bill presented to parliament has some effect with respect to a public charge. Even the cost of printing it is one, in itself.
The whole point we are to determine, of course, is how remote the charge is, and as it becomes more remote, then it does not come within the requirements of the resolution. And as both hon. members have pointed out, they have to argue that it is possible that there might be a charge, despite the care with which the amendment was drafted, to impose upon the Postmaster General certain obligations to see that a charge did not in fact occur. Now it was not entirely an oversight that this was drafted in that way-though I am not suggesting that we had in mind bringing this in at that time.
Let me make some brief references to additional material supplied by the hon. member for Kamloops about the supposed motives we might have had under these circumstances. This amendment-and I frankly confess it-was not available at the time the resolution was drafted. I do not suggest that, if it had been, it might necessarily have been included in the resolution. But we desire to put this in at this time for the very obvious reason that the Post Office Act is now being amended, and it is more convenient to do it in this manner-subject to what I shall say in a moment-and that it is proper to do so, in order to avoid duplication of debate in the house.
The question of surprise is the only one upon which I have anything to say, or concerning which 1 have any sympathy in respect of the arguments made by my hon. friends. A new clause will not be entertained if it is beyond the scope of a bill, inconsistent with clauses agreed to by the committee, or substantially the same as a clause previously negatived.
I would also like to draw to the attention of the committee citation 678 of the same edition, which reads as follows:
Amendments cannot be moved which are based on schedules or other provisions, the terms of which have not been placed before the committee.
And then in citation 679 of Beauchesne's third edition there appears the following:
Amendments are out or order if they are (a) irrelevant to the bill, or beyond its scope, governed by or dependent upon amendments already negatived:
The minister has drawn my attention to citation 681 and in his remarks he mentioned the wide powers for amendment in committee. There were several matters which were discussed yesterday with reference to employment and to the manner in which the provisions of the 40-hour week would be implemented with regard to the employment of casual labour. At that time the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) remarked that the liquidation staffs which had been

Post Office Act
handling the carriage of mail during the liquidation time of the letter carriers would be absorbed into the letter sorting department.
I rather doubted that. I doubted that they could absorb these people, and I made some inquiries. So far as I can tell, from the information which is available to me, they will not be able to absorb anywhere near the number of men who have been serving on the liquidation staffs. I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the maximum hourly rate now earned by letter carriers is $1.33 an hour, and that under the new regulations with respect to the 40-hour week the maximum rate earned by letter carriers will be $1.47 an hour. Yet these are the men who are being asked to volunteer to come back on Saturdays for a dollar an hour, to do their own work.
Mr. Speaker, all during this whole debate I have consistently objected to the passage of this bill, the manner in which it was brought in, and the blame which was being placed on the changed working conditions of letter carriers and others in the department. Now I must say once more that in my opinion this is a most deplorable situation, when men who have established working conditions and have established their procedure over many years are being asked, in effect, to work extra time at about three-quarters of their regular rate.
I doubt very much whether there is any industry in the country which would have the temerity to suggest to its employees that they should come in and work overtime at 75 per cent of their regular rate. I do not think the Post Office Department has any right even to make this suggestion to its employees. I think it is a despicable thing to try to undermine the working conditions of your own employees by making this suggestion, trading on the possibility that there might be a few employees, here and there, who would do practically anything to earn a few extra dollars per week. There are people who will do that; they are desperately in need of money, for one reason or another, and they will take whatever offers.
The idea of bringing in casual labour, mixing them up with the regular postal employees; the idea of saying to the postal staff that it is understood that if the occasion arises the postmaster has the authority to order any employee to work on Saturdays if he fails to volunteer, and to say further that absenteeism will not be condoned- these things practically amount to a threat, Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand the thinking in a department which will make such suggestions to its employees.

There are other things which should have been brought out on clause 1 of the bill, and if I was not quick enough to catch the intent of the chairman then I must accept the blame for my shortcomings. I would have liked to ask the Postmaster General some questions, but I cannot do that now on third reading. However, I understand that T.C.A. is carrying mail not only in its luggage compartments but in passenger seats. I understand that there is carriage of papers and magazines in passenger seats, and that there is some sort of arrangement between the post office and T.C.A. to do that very thing. These are matters that should have come out at the committee stage of the bill; they are matters on which I have notes and had intended to raise. That is why I was so anxious to have this matter reopened this afternoon.
We have been debating this matter for some time now, Mr. Speaker, and at no time have we ever conceded that there was any virtue in this bill. We have had a couple of amendments proposed and voted on, and we have lost them. But in the course of the debate we have heard some of the recommendations which were proposed by the Woods and Gordon company. We have not had any satisfactory answer as to which of these recommendations have been implemented or are to be implemented, or as to the savings which might reasonably be effected. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, at this time I move, seconded by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks):
That this bill be not now read a third time but that further consideration thereof be postponed until such time as the house is in a position to assess the effects of the implementation of the J. D. Woods and Gordon report.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 2, consideration of the motion of Mr, Campbell, for the second reading of Bill No. 175, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act (protection of rivers).

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO ENLARGE SCOPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned on Tuesday of last week I was discussing the bill sponsored by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell), and I was attempting to show at that time that what the hon. member was trying to do was to amend an act concerning navigation, over which the federal government alone has jurisdiction, by virtue of the British North America Act, to remedy the pollution of certain waters, a matter which falls normally for determination under provincial jurisdiction. I had gone on to explain that his amendment to the act together with the amendment moved by the hon. member for

Navigable Waters Protection Act Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) accentuated the position. I had summed up by casting doubt on the constitutionality of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Prince Albert.
Since then I have had the opportunity of considering the bill, together with the amendment brought forward by the hon. member for Prince Albert, and now I have no hesitation in stating unequivocally that the amendment leaves no doubt in my mind as to its invalidity. I should like to quote the words which the hon. member for Prince Albert sought to introduce to the bill proposed by the hon. member for The Battlefords. The hon. member for Prince Albert moved:
That after the word "whatsoever" in the fifth line of section 18 in the bill the following words be added:
"or chemicals of any kind, and without restricting the generality of the foregoing any substance which, although not deleterious or harmful to human health, causes discomfort or annoyance to risers of water."
In order that there may be some sequence in the debate, and since the bill is a short one, perhaps I may read it now as it would stand amended:
Section 18 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, chapter 193 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
18. No owner or tenant of any sawmill, or other industrial plant, or any workman therein or other person shall throw or cause to be thrown, or suffer or permit to be thrown any sawdust, edgings, slabs, bark or rubbish of any description whatsoever, or chemicals of any kind, and without restricting the generality of the foregoing any substance which, although not deleterious or harmful to human health, causes discomfort or annoyance to users of water.
In my understanding it now becomes quite clear that the amendment is one that has to do with the pollution of water, one that has to do with the drinking of water, and unquestionably one that has to do with health, a matter which is entirely extraneous to navigation and shipping and over which the Navigable Waters Protection Act would have no jurisdiction whatsoever.
The bill in itself is ineffective, in my opinion, to remedy the situation, unless it can be shown that these deleterious matters, or the industrial plants to which my hon. friend refers, have to do with navigation and shipping. If he can connect them up with the fact that these matters interfere with navigation and shipping, then of course there would be jurisdiction; but no one, I think, will argue that chemicals interfere with shipping. I do not think they do. Neither is it the property of a chemical to interfere with navigation, and I do not think there is any


way in which you can link those chemicals or deleterious matters with navigation and shipping.
If I go a step farther and use the argument of the hon. member for The Battlefords, I think he will agree with me in this conclusion; because if one looks at Hansard for February 2, at page 1702 he will see this stated by the hon. member:
The discussion to which the minister referred related to an amendment moved by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) to section 19 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and had to do with the pollution of the waters along the shore line of lake Ontario, while the case which I am arguing refers to a river running through three provinces. During that debate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) argued that the federal government was not competent to deal with the situation, and the amendment was voted down. I believe the minister was correct, because this is a completely different situation.
But it is not. There is no difference at all between the situation to which my hon. friend refers and that argued by the hon. member for York West. The position is exactly the same. The fact that three provinces are involved does not alter the jurisdiction of the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Even if there were ten provinces it would make absolutely no difference in so far as this act is concerned. It would give no jurisdiction over navigation. It might make some difference in so far as the question of health is concerned, but that is not a matter for me to determine. As I said earlier, this matter is one which comes under navigation and shipping and I am concerned only with that aspect of it at the moment, because that is the only aspect which my hon. friend seeks to consider in his anxiety to meet the difficult position in which the people of Prince Albert and other communities along the shores of the North Saskatchewan river find themselves.
I have a great deal of sympathy for the position in which he and other hon. members find themselves at the moment, but I am sure that he and the other hon. members would not want an act to be passed which would be ultra vires; for, after all, what would be the use of passing an act if we knew in advance that it would not meet the position and would not be intra vires of the British North America Act?
That brings me to the statement made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The leader of the C.C.F. party said at page 1705 of Hansard:
Now, the Saskatchewan river is frequented by fish. Is it more important to protect the lives and the health of fish than the lives and the health of people who live along this river?

The answer of course is no. It is far more important to protect the lives of humans than it is to protect the lives of fish, but if we have no jurisdiction to protect the lives of humans under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, then why enact legislation when we know beforehand, as I said earlier, that the legislation would be innocuous?
Again, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar asked why we did not do something under sections 32 and 33 of the Fisheries Act. I believe the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) dealt with that matter earlier, when in answer to a question in the house he said that while under the British North America Act legislative jurisdiction over fisheries lay with the federal government, since 1930, by agreement with the provinces, they were the ones who administered their own natural resources, including fisheries. I think he made it quite clear that if some remedy were desired, perhaps the best way to seek that remedy was to consult those who had been administering the act for some years.
I conclude by reiterating what I have said already, that while there will be a great deal of concern for the problems which hon. members have spoken about in this debate and for which a remedy is sought, and while there will be a great deal of sympathy and much concern for the people themselves, I do not think the house or any hon. member in the house would want to suggest a remedy which would have no effect. I have no hesitation in saying that the amendment brought forward by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in my humble opinion would not meet the position from a constitutional standpoint and is ultra vires.
So far as the argument of the hon. member for The Battlefords is concerned, I can see no difference whatsoever between this attempt to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and the attempt made by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) on an earlier occasion. I have forgotten what reasons I gave, or whether I had consulted the Department of Justice at that time, but my recollection is that I had and that the deputy minister of justice gave as his opinion that it would not be possible to make the amendment within the constitution. Again, I do not think there is any difference between what is attempted here and what was attempted on that occasion.
I remind hon. members that I am not attempting to deal with the problem as regards health. That is not a matter that concerns the navigation of ships or shipping on navigable waters. I am concerned only
Navigable Waters Protection Act with the operation of that act, and I say that to attempt to deal with the matter, which is chiefly provincial, by amending this act would in my opinion be ultra vires.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. Robertson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO ENLARGE SCOPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) who is unavoidably absent because of other important government business, I would like to make a few comments on this bill.
This bill, introduced by the hon. member for The Battlefords, seeks to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. By so doing I understand he is seeking to give the federal government authority to deal with a very disturbing problem in his area. This problem has been the subject matter of a number of questions put to the Minister of National Health and Welfare by the hon. member for The Battlefords and the hon. member for Prince Albert during the past month. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has indicated his concern over this matter, and he has pointed out that we have no jurisdiction to deal with it.
Nevertheless, he has offered the full co-operation of the department in assisting the provinces to correct this very unfortunate situation. On February 2 the hon. member for The Battlefords moved an amendment by this bill. It has been pointed out very ably by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chev-rier) that this would amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act, a subject dealing with navigation over which the federal government has jurisdiction; that in fact we are being asked to remedy a situation which is a health matter, namely the pollution of the water used in those areas. In my opinion also, this matter should be dealt with in another way, and further I would state that this matter comes under the jurisdiction of the provincial government.
This problem has to deal with the dumping of industrial waste into the North Saskatchewan river which provides water for some
1928	HOUSE OF
Navigable Waters Protection Act of the cities in the hon. member's constituency, namely the cities of North Battle-ford and Prince Albert, and the town of Battleford. I am sure we all sympathize with the hon. member and with the people living in those areas because they are being subjected to a very disagreeable situation. As a result of these substances being dumped into the North Saskatchewan river we know that the water in the cities I have mentioned has a very objectionable odour and taste, and I am informed that this extends as far as The Pas in Manitoba.
I have seen many of the reports which have come to our department, and so far there is no report which indicates there is an associated health hazard. I would not minimize the distress which is being caused to the people in these areas, but I think that is an important point to make. On previous occasions the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has indicated the action taken by our department. This action has been taken by the Department of National Health and Welfare in conjunction with the provinces concerned because, as I have stated and as the minister has stated on many occasions, we believe that this is a matter coming under provincial jurisdiction; and further, the provinces themselves are quite agreed that it is their responsibility.
I should like to outline what the Department of National Health and Welfare has done to correct this situation. At the request of the provincial health officers we have sent the supervising engineer of the division of public health engineering in our department to consult with officials of the various provinces concerned. He has talked with officials of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. He has also taken part in conferences, at which industries concerned attended, and he has given to those officials the benefit of his experience.
The occupational health laboratory of our division have also been working on this problem. They have examined samples of the water taken from various cities in that locality, and are giving the provinces the benefit of their advice. We have also attempted to obtain all possible information from the United States. We have been in touch with the environmental health centre at Cincinnati, asking them to give us the benefit of their experience in dealing with such matters. We have been assured that such help will be forthcoming in the very near future. I therefore hope all hon. members will agree that our department has been extremely sympathetic in connection with the difficulty and have taken concrete steps to correct it.


I should like to point out that the solution of this problem is most complicated. We have yet been unable to identify the offending substance, or substances, or combination of substances which are related to this problem and which are the cause of this disagreeable condition, nor have we been able to say what their origin is. It will only be by intensive research that it will be possible to determine the cause. In fact there may be a number of substances involved. They made be coming from more than one source. More than one industry may be involved. The solution is not likely to be simple. It will require exhaustive studies of a highly technical and specialized kind to determine the real source of this trouble.
It might appear that the obvious solution to this problem might consist in closing down some of these industries; but I am sure that, on reflection, this would not be termed a particularly satisfactory solution. It might require the closing down of a great number of industries. In addition to the economic implications, we have no assurance that this would be a permanent solution to the problem.
While we are attempting to identify the substances concerned, temporary measures have been taken to deal with this situation. In one locality, the use of activated charcoal has been useful in clearing up this condition. I am told that laboratory tests indicate that chlorine dioxide might be useful in purifying the water. I am also informed that one locality is considering the use of this substance.
I hope I have made it clear that the solution is not to be found in jurisdictional responsibility, but that it will require the intensive efforts and the co-operation of all people concerned in order to find a satisfactory solution to this problem. If the provinces concerned-and notably the province of Alberta, where the difficulty seems to originate-will agree, the minister is prepared to make available the services of the technical officers of our department to cooperate with the provinces and the industries concerned in setting up and engaging in the co-ordinated investigation which we believe is essential.
As the minister indicated to the house a few days ago, he dispatched a telegram to the minister of health in the province of Alberta offering the full facilities of our department to the province in attempting to correct this situation. I may once again refer to the telegram which the minister read to the house on that occasion:
In view of the many questions asked respecting the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river through industrial wastes said to originate with

industries in Alberta, I would like to offer the co-operation and assistance of the technical officers of this department to participate in a joint study with the technical officers of your province and of the industries to endeavour to find a solution to the problem. I appreciate that the matter is not one that is within federal responsibility but in view of its importance and the complications and technical difficulties that would appear to exist, the solution may well be one that can only be found with the full utilization of all of the technical resources that can be made available. If you feel that this is a helpful proposal I suggest that you have Dr. Somerville communicate with Dr. Cameron with a view to working out satisfactory details and arrangements for an immediate study.
The house is aware that today the Minister *of National Health and Welfare informed the house that Dr. Somerville, who is deputy minister of health in the province of Alberta, telephoned Dr. Cameron, the deputy minister of our department, informing him that the province of Alberta was most anxious to co-operate in every way it could. He also expressed his appreciation of the helpful assistance which has been forthcoming from the Department of National Health and Welfare. The minister also informed the house that he was in conversation with the minister of health of the province of Saskatchewan and that he too is most anxious to co-operate in the solution of this problem.
The minister has also directed that all possible speed be taken to place the facilities of our department at the service of the provinces. Already the staffs of the public health engineering division and the occupational health division of our department are taking the necessary steps to assist the provinces with this work. It will be necessary to divert some of the staff of these two divisions from important work which they are now carrying on, but it is felt that it is most necessary in order to assist the provinces with this matter. I am also informed that it is not likely that a solution can be found in a short time. As I have indicated, it is a complex situation and it is felt that it may be some time before a definite solution is found.
I should like to emphasize that the success of any effort in dealing with this problem is dependent upon the co-operation of all of the industries that may be involved. We assume that this co-operation will be forthcoming from those industries, and that they are as anxious as anyone else to clear up the situation. The measures which may be found necessary for control, once a solution is found, and the enforcement of those measures must, of course, remain the responsibility of the provinces.
I am sure all hon. members agree that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has
Navigable Waters Protection Act shown much understanding of the situation that prevails, and that he has been most helpful in co-ordinating the work of the various governments in attempting to find a solution to this very important problem.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO ENLARGE SCOPE
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this bill.
I feel that the hon. member for The Battle-fords (Mr. Campbell) should be congratulated on introducing it. Having given it some study, I must say that I agree with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that the bill will not bring about what the hon. member for The Battlefords is seeking. The-Navigable Waters Protection Act has to do with navigation; therefore I do not think any pollution that might affect the health of people can be remedied under it.
I think it is a good thing to have this, matter brought before the house. The situation in the west is serious, and is one that, may arise in other parts of Canada. I believe some thought should be given to it. by the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Justice from the point of view of trying to work out some arrangements with the provinces whereby there might be a conference or some other action to take care of such situations in the future. This may be the first time this situation has. arisen, but it will not be the last.
Not long ago a somewhat similar problem arose in eastern Canada, and it is not the first time we have had this trouble. It. has been brought to the attention of one or two departments. I believe the Department, of Fisheries knows about it. However, this case in the east is different in that it involves international waters. The river rises in Canada, flows through the state of Maine and then re-enters Canada, and the water is polluted. There is no remedy under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Large numbers of fish were killed last summer, and the doctor in charge of health matters.
1930	HOUSE OF
Navigable Waters Protection Act there said that as far as he could tell the cause was pollution of the water in the state of Maine, but there does not seem to be anyway of rectifying it.
I know that is a different problem from an interprovincial one, but it does place emphasis on the question. In a large country such as ours we have interprovincial rivers and international waters. As our country develops, industrial plants are going to be built adjacent to these waters, and in my opinion it is time for some thought to be given to the working out of a convention or agreement among the provinces and the dominion government whereby machinery will be provided so these problems can be dealt with speedily, especially where the health of our people is concerned.
I am sorry I cannot say very much in favour of this particular bill as something to meet the requirements of the hon. member.
I do not see much objection to what is in it, but it is not going to help meet the situation so far as health or pollution is concerned, because the material that seems to be in the waters of this western river is not material that interferes with navigation. Looking at the bill from a legal standpoint, it is not going to meet the ends the hon. member has in mind. Nevertheless he has brought a most important matter before the house, and it should receive a lot of thought and consideration so that similar situations may be met when they arise in the future. Consideration should also be given to the problem that arises when international waters are involved, because there does not seem to be any machinery to deal with such matters effectively.

speechtext:

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to remove the limits on the compensation payable in respect of swine and sheep, and to provide for payment of compensation on the basis of market value.

subtopic: CHANGE IN BASIS OF COMPENSATION IN RESPECT OF SWINE AND SHEEP
speechtext: Is the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture going to explain the resolution?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CHANGE IN BASIS OF COMPENSATION IN RESPECT OF SWINE AND SHEEP
speechtext:
The reason for the introduction of this resolution, Mr. Chairman, upon which the bill is founded, is to compensate the owners of hogs which have been slaughtered as a result of the outbreak of hog cholera. As we all know, hog cholera is the disease which hog producers, not only in Canada but in other countries as well, fear most. Heretofore the compensation which has been paid for a hog has been $30 or any portion thereof according to the value of the hog. If a hog were worth $50 or more, as it is now when it is ready for market, the owner was compensated only to the extent of $30 if the animal were slaughtered under the terms of this act. The government felt that some increased compensation should be given to a man who was in that position, and had hogs ready or

nearly ready for market which had to be slaughtered. We are introducing the resolution to compensate him more adequately.

subtopic: CHANGE IN BASIS OF COMPENSATION IN RESPECT OF SWINE AND SHEEP
speechtext:
I do not intend to say very much at the resolution stage. I should like to say, first, that I believe this measure is long overdue. I noticed that the parliamentary assistant just mentioned hogs, but the resolution also speaks of sheep. I believe that the compensation paid for sheep in the past has been much too low, especially for purebred animals. It is extremely difficult to arrive at the real value of purebred animals, and of course we shall have to wait until we get the bill before we can ascertain the basis for fixing the value. If it is similar to the basis for cattle, then I believe it is probably fair.
In some cases the compensation is not enough because it is a stipulated amount, plus the value of the carcass where it is suitable for consumption. In the case of highly bred animals, that is not enough. We all realize that, but it is rather difficult to arrive at any hard and fast rule. We shall reserve further comments until we see the contents of the bill.

subtopic: CHANGE IN BASIS OF COMPENSATION IN RESPECT OF SWINE AND SHEEP
speechtext:
I do
not want to say very much at the resolution stage, except to ask the parliamentary assistant if any consideration has been given to increasing the compensation to those who have to dispose of purebred hogs? If the government is considering an amendment to this act, has consideration been given to increasing the compensation paid to cattle breeders who suffer the loss of purebred cattle?
I should like to point out to the parliamentary assistant and the house that in the case of purebred cattle, the compensation under the act today stands at a maximum of $100. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution will introduce a bill to give legislative effect to the northwest Atlantic fisheries convention, which was approved by this house in July, 1950.
This is one of the series of international fisheries conventions which this country has been able to arrange for the proper protection and conservation of the fisheries on the high seas adjacent to our shores. The first was the international halibut convention, signed in 1923, covering the halibut of the north Pacific, followed by the fur seal convention and the international salmon convention. Then last year a new convention for control of the north Pacific was signed by Japan, Canada and the United States.
The area covered by the convention of this resolution is the northwest Atlantic, with the Grand Banks the principal fishery concerned. The Grand Banks are still, after 400 years of fishing, the greatest single fishery in the world, but in recent years there have been signs of depletion in one or two of the banks, which gave concern to the nations which are fishing that great fishing ground. Just after the war, meetings were arranged between those nations, and as a consequence we had this convention, which was approved by parliament. The ten nations are Canada, Denmark, Iceland, Italy, France, Norway, Portugal, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Since the convention was approved in this house an administrative organization has been established. I am happy to report that because of the very attractive proposals made to the new commission by the government of Nova Scotia and the governors of Dalhousie University, the permanent headquarters of this new northwest Atlantic commission have been located at Halifax on the campus of Dalhousie University. The first chairman of this commission is our own Canadian deputy minister of fisheries, Stewart Bates, who was also honoured last week by being elected the first chairman of the new north Pacific international fisheries commission.
The commission has drafted regulations to enforce conservation measures on these banks. Now we have come to parliament to give us legal power to enforce these regulations on Canadian fishermen.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the boundary line between Ontario and Manitoba has been completely surveyed and marked on the ground by commissioners appointed from time to time by the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and Canada. The two provinces have requested that the parliament of Canada pass legislation confirming the boundary, and for this purpose they have themselves passed the required legislation.
The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to confirm the boundary between the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba in compliance with their respective requests and in accordance with the British North America Act.
In these days of the rapid development of mining and other industries, particularly in the northern section of our provinces and in the territories, it is imperative that boundary lines between the provinces be as firmly and clearly established as possible. This is vitally important not only to the provinces and territories but to the private firms and private citizens who are helping to open up new areas to development and settlement. The bill before the house is a helpful step in that direction. It seeks to establish with certainty the boundary between Ontario and Manitoba.
The history of the determination of this boundary is rather long and complicated. As a measure of assistance to this house I shall attempt to summarize briefly the historical background of this particular interprovincial boundary line, the total length of which is 609 miles.
As early as 1870 in the case of Manitoba and 1889 in the case of Ontario, the boundaries of these provinces were originally defined by statutes for the respective provinces. In 1893 an unsuccessful attempt was
Ontario-Manitoba Boundary Act made by the then secretary of state for Canada to arrange with the two provinces for a survey of the boundary between them on a co-operative basis. Manitoba declined the invitation at that time, as that province did not then have the ownership of its natural resources. But Ontario did accept. As a result a commission was established composed of one representative from Ontario and one from the federal authority. This commission in 1897 and 1898 surveyed and marked a portion of the boundary.
At this stage the federal deputy minister of justice was asked to advise what further steps could properly be taken to establish the boundary between Ontario and Manitoba. The advice was given in the following terms:
The boundary line between Ontario and Manitoba, as marked on the ground by Messrs. Stewart and Saunders, can be absolutely established only by legislation. If the legislatures of Ontario and Manitoba consent, the parliament of Canada can, by the provisions of the British North America Act, 1871, pass an act declaring that line to be the boundary between the two provinces. Orders in council of the several governments accepting the line might be passed, but these would not bind the provincial legislatures or parliament of Canada.
On October 10, 1898, the two provinces were invited to accept the boundary as marked by commissioners Stewart and Saunders. Ontario accepted the invitation and passed 62 Victoria, chapter 2. It does not appear that Manitoba passed any legislation on the matter at that time. In the absence of Manitoba's consent, no legislation was passed by the federal government.
In 1921 the two provinces were again invited to join in a continuation of the boundary line survey. Manitoba declined. Accordingly, the governments of Canada and Ontario each appointed a representative and survey work was extended to the twelfth base line and reached completion in 1921-22.
In 1929 both Manitoba and Ontario passed acts of consent, accepting and confirming as the true and unalterable boundary between the two provinces the survey that had been made by the two commissioners and marked on the ground from the northwest angle of the lake of the Woods to the twelfth base line.
The parliament of Canada did not pass any legislation at that time to confirm that part of the boundary because it was thought advisable, I am informed, to wait until the boundary was completely surveyed and marked. The last part of the boundary, from the twelfth base line to the shores of Hudson bay, have since been surveyed and marked by monuments of a permanent nature under the supervision of commissioners appointed by Manitoba, Ontario and Canada.	.

Ontario-Manitoba Boundary Act
The two provinces have expressed the wish that the boundary line thus surveyed and marked be accepted and confirmed. Both provinces have passed acts consenting to a declaration to that effect by the parliament of Canada. The purpose of this bill is to carry into legislative effect the request of Ontario and Manitoba, and it is also in accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the British North America Act, 1871.

Explosives Act
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Explosives Act, Which the bill now before the house amends in several particulars, has had a relatively recent history. The act was first introduced in parliament in 1911, and did not pass through all its stages before the session of that year concluded. The act was again introduced in 1914 and was passed that year. Proclamation of the measure was delayed on account of world war I until 1920. The original Explosives Act was based on the British North America Act of 1875. The purpose of the legislation is to provide a measure of control in the manufacture, testing, storage and importation of explosives in the interests of public safety.
The 1914 act, proclaimed, as I have said, in 1920, continued in operation until 1946. In that year it was revised because of postwar conditions. During the course of world war II a number of regulations were made under the War Measures Act in order to secure closer and more effective control over explosives. It has become advisable to recommend a number of new amendments at this time. One of these is to make clear that the Explosives Act applies to government agencies as well as to private firms and individual citizens charged with the use or control of explosives. The amendments include a broadening of the definition of "factory" to include land adjacent to the site where the manufacture of explosives is carried on, also all buildings on the said site.
The terms of licences under the act are dealt with as well as certain regulatory measures covering the importation and manufacture of explosives in order not to endanger public safety. The amendments deal with such matters as the inspection of magazines and the destruction of explosives which appear to be abandoned or in a position to be dangerous to persons and property. During the 33 years in which the act has been in force it has proved of value as a public safeguard.
Hon. members will appreciate that in the post-war period of expansion widespread use was made of various types of explosives. As a result of this act the quality and uniformity of explosives marketed in Canada have greatly improved. Although the use of explosives marketed in Canada has quadrupled since the act was first passed the number of accidents has shown a steady decline, owing to the control exercised by inspectors of explosives under this legislation. I might add that the manufacturers have also co-operated toward this end.

I notice that the purpose of this clause is to enlarge the definition of "factory" to include the site on which the factory stands. The present section reads:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTS, OFFENCES, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext:
This amendment is based on experience under the act. I am informed that when the word "factory" was first defined it was intended to cover by the definition not only the buildings in which the manufacture or any part of the process of manufacture of explosives is carried on but also all other buildings on the site and the site itself. The definition as it now reads seems to cover only buildings in which an explosive is manufactured or stored.
In a recent case in Ontario a person was found in the boiler room of a factory. The person was charged under section 21 of the act with trespassing upon the factory. The case was heard and the accused was found not guilty. Among the reasons given in the judgment one was that the accused, not being in a building where any part of the process of manufacture of an explosive was carried on, was not guilty of the offence with which he was charged. This amendment is to clarify that section and make sure that anyone trespassing on the premises will be liable as a trespasser.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTS, OFFENCES, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext:
On Thursday we shall continue with this debate. When it is concluded we shall take second reading of the bill to amend the Patent Act; then second reading of the bill respecting the Canadian forces, the bill respecting benefits for members of the Canadian forces, the bill respecting the War Service Grants Act, the bill respecting
the national battlefields at Quebec, the bill with respect to the northwest Atlantic fisheries as a consequence of the resolution having passed tonight, and then second reading of the bill to amend the Telegraphs Act. It has been suggested that on Friday we might consider the Criminal Code throughout the day.

speechtext: At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
